{"id": "57817c83-2917-40bb-b14c-6d2b5005313c", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Lifecycle rules cut S3 costs by moving objects to cheaper storage classes as they age and by deleting data you no longer need. These are the changes that usually save the most, roughly in order of payoff.

## 1. Clean up waste first
These rules are cheap to add, and they carry little risk.
- **Abort incomplete multipart uploads.** Failed uploads leave hidden parts that you still pay for. A rule that aborts them after 7 days or less is almost always worth adding.
- **Expire noncurrent versions.** On versioned buckets, old versions pile up quietly. Expire them after 30 to 90 days. You can also keep only the newest N noncurrent versions.
- **Remove expired delete markers.** This stops orphaned markers from cluttering the bucket and slowing listings.
- **Expire temporary data.** Logs, temp files, exports and build artifacts can be scoped by prefix or tag and deleted after a set number of days.

## 2. Transition data as it cools
Pick the target class based on how the data is accessed:

| Access pattern | Good target |
|---|---|
| Unknown or changing | **Intelligent-Tiering.** It moves objects between tiers automatically and has no retrieval fees. |
| Infrequent, but needs millisecond access | **Standard-IA** (or One Zone-IA if you can accept a single AZ) |
| Archive, but occasionally needs fast access | **Glacier Instant Retrieval** |
| Archive, with retrieval in minutes to hours | **Glacier Flexible Retrieval** |
| Long-term compliance data that's rarely read | **Glacier Deep Archive** |

A common pattern is Standard → Standard-IA at 30 days → Glacier at 90 days → Deep Archive at 180 days or more, with an expiration at your retention limit. You can apply the same transitions to noncurrent versions.

## 3. Check the constraints so you don't pay more
- **Small objects.** By default, lifecycle rules don't transition objects under **128 KB**. Millions of tiny objects won't benefit, and per-request transition charges can outweigh the savings. Use an object-size filter to include or exclude them on purpose.
- **Transition request charges.** Each object moved costs a per-request fee, so transitioning huge numbers of small objects can be a net loss.
- **Minimum storage durations.** The IA classes charge for at least 30 days and Glacier classes for 90 days. Deep Archive charges for at least 180 days. Deleting or moving objects sooner still bills the remainder.
- **Retrieval fees and latency.** IA and Glacier classes charge to read data. Don't archive anything your application reads often.
- **Expirations are permanent.** Consider turning on versioning, or testing on a narrow prefix first, before enabling broad delete rules.
- Billing updates as if transitions and expirations happened immediately, even though S3 processes them asynchronously.

## 4. Find where to apply rules
Before writing rules, look at what is actually costing you money:
- **S3 Storage Lens** shows incomplete multipart upload bytes, noncurrent version bytes, and cold prefixes across all buckets.
- **Storage Class Analysis** on a bucket or prefix tells you when data stops being accessed, which tells you when to transition.
- **Cost Explorer** or **Cost and Usage Reports** show which buckets and storage classes dominate your bill.

## Example rule (JSON)
```json
{
  "Rules": [{
    "ID": "tier-and-clean-logs",
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
    "Transitions": [
      { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
      { "Days": 90, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
    ],
    "Expiration": { "Days": 365 },
    "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30 },
    "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
  }]
}
```
Apply it with `aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration`. Applying it replaces the bucket's whole lifecycle configuration, so include any existing rules.

I can look at your buckets for you. I can check which have versioning, existing lifecycle rules, or large storage in Standard, and where the cleanup opportunities are. Tell me if you want that.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

- **Small objects.** By default, lifecycle rules don't transition objects under **128 KB**. Millions of tiny objects won't benefit, and per-request transition charges can outweigh the savings. Use an object-size filter to include or exclude them on purpose.
- **Transition request charges.** Each object moved costs a per-request fee, so transitioning huge numbers of small objects can be a net loss.
- **Minimum storage durations.** The IA classes charge for at least 30 days and Glacier classes for 90 days. Deep Archive charges for at least 180 days. Deleting or moving objects sooner still bills the remainder.
- **Retrieval fees and latency.** IA and Glacier classes charge to read data. Don't archive anything your application reads often.
- **Expirations are permanent.** Consider turning on versioning, or testing on a narrow prefix first, before enabling broad delete rules.
- Billing updates as if transitions and expirations happened immediately, even though S3 processes them asynchronously.

## 4. Find where to apply rules
Before writing rules, look at what is actually costing you money:
- **S3 Storage Lens** shows incomplete multipart upload bytes, noncurrent version bytes, and cold prefixes across all buckets.
- **Storage Class Analysis** on a bucket or prefix tells you when data stops being accessed, which tells you when to transition.
- **Cost Explorer** or **Cost and Usage Reports** show which buckets and storage classes dominate your bill.
